title: Register a LiblineaR engine for multinom_reg()
description:
`logistic_reg()` now errors when the outcome has more than two levels (#1444), with one exception: the `"LiblineaR"` engine is allowed through.

The exception exists because LiblineaR genuinely fits a correct multiclass model:

```r
library(parsnip)
f <- logistic_reg() |> set_engine("LiblineaR") |> fit(Species ~ ., data = iris)
predict(f, iris[c(1, 51, 101), ], type = "prob")
#>   .pred_setosa .pred_versicolor .pred_virginica
#> 1        0.878            0.122           0.000
#> 2        0.032            0.859           0.109
#> 3        0.000            0.145           0.854

predict(f, iris[c(1, 51, 101), ], type = "class")$.pred_class
#> [1] setosa     versicolor virginica
```

Rows sum to 1 and all three classes are predicted correctly. Erroring there would remove working functionality, and `multinom_reg()` has no LiblineaR engine to redirect those users to:

```r
unique(parsnip:::get_from_env("multinom_reg")$engine)
#> [1] "glmnet" "spark"  "keras"  "keras3" "nnet"   "brulee"
```

## Suggestion

Register `"LiblineaR"` as an engine for `multinom_reg()`. `LiblineaR::LiblineaR()` is already the fit function used by `logistic_reg()` and `svm_linear()`, so the registration should be largely mechanical — the multiclass behaviour is what the solver does by default when given a factor with more than two levels.

Once that exists, the carve-out in `check_outcome()` can be removed and `logistic_reg()` can error uniformly, which is the cleaner end state: the model function name would then always mean what it says, and the error's advice to "use `multinom_reg()`" would be actionable for every engine.

## Note

Worth confirming which of LiblineaR's solver `type` values are appropriate for multiclass before registering, and whether `predict(type = "prob")` is available for all of them — `svm_linear()`'s LiblineaR engine has no probability support, so the two registrations should not be assumed to be symmetric.

title: bart() classification silently accepts outcomes that are not binary
description:
`bart()` classification with the `"dbarts"` engine accepts an outcome with any number of levels. dbarts models a *binary* outcome, and parsnip hands it the factor codes without checking, so anything other than exactly two levels silently produces invalid results.

## Genuinely multiclass

```r
library(parsnip)
set.seed(1)
fit3 <- bart(trees = 5) |>
  set_engine("dbarts") |>
  set_mode("classification") |>
  fit(Species ~ ., data = iris)          # fits without complaint

predict(fit3, iris[c(1, 51, 101), ], type = "prob")
#>   .pred_setosa .pred_versicolor
#> 1        0.998            0.002
#> 2        0.006            0.994
#> 3       -1.002            2.002        # <- not probabilities
```

Three things are wrong at once: the values are outside `[0, 1]`, there are only two columns for a three-level outcome, and `virginica` — a level that *is* in the data — is missing entirely while the reported columns are mislabelled.

The cause is visible in what dbarts receives:

```r
sort(unique(fit3$fit$y))
#> [1] 0 1 2
```

dbarts expects `0`/`1`. Given `0`/`1`/`2` it fits something meaningless.

## Two used levels, but an unused level retained

The same root cause bites a binary outcome that has not been `droplevels()`ed, and how it fails depends on where the unused level sits.

Unused level **last** — `class` and `prob` happen to be right, but interval predictions error:

```r
dat <- iris[iris$Species != "virginica", ]   # keeps unused "virginica"
f <- bart(trees = 5) |> set_engine("dbarts") |> set_mode("classification") |>
  fit(Species ~ ., data = dat)

predict(f, dat[1:3, ], type = "conf_int")
#> Error in `rlang::set_names()`:
#> ! The size of `nm` (6) must be compatible with the size of `x` (4).
```

`obj$lvl` has three entries, so `paste0(".pred_lower_", obj$lvl)` generates six names for a four-column tibble.

Unused level **first** — silently wrong instead, because the factor codes become `1`/`2` rather than `0`/`1`:

```r
d <- iris[iris$Species != "setosa", ]
d$Species <- factor(d$Species, levels = levels(iris$Species))
f2 <- bart(trees = 5) |> set_engine("dbarts") |> set_mode("classification") |>
  fit(Species ~ ., data = d)

predict(f2, d[c(1, 60), ], type = "prob")
#>   .pred_setosa .pred_versicolor
#> 1        0.002            0.998
#> 2       -1.001            2.001

predict(f2, d[c(1, 60), ], type = "class")$.pred_class
#> [1] versicolor versicolor       # second observation is virginica
```

## Suggested fix

Check at fit time rather than trying to repair this at predict time, since the fitted model is already meaningless by then. `check_outcome()` in `R/misc.R` is the natural place: it receives both `y` and the spec, and already carries a precedent in the `logistic_reg` + more-than-two-levels case immediately below.

The two situations warrant different advice, so it is worth distinguishing them: when exactly two levels are present in the data the fix is `droplevels()`, and when more than two are genuinely used the model simply cannot fit it.

Unlike the `logistic_reg` case — which warns, because some engines bin the extra levels — this should error. There is no reading under which a "probability" of `2.002` was intended.

## Notes

Found while fixing #1407, which flagged the `set_names()` error as a separate, out-of-scope problem. This is that problem, plus the silently-wrong cases behind it.

`bart()` currently registers only the dbarts engine, so scoping the check to `bart` + `"dbarts"` avoids blocking a future engine that does support multiclass.

title: add new model ordinal_reg() for ordinal regression
description:
This was discussed in two previous issues, #35 and #953. The new model is being added in [this fork branch](https://github.com/corybrunson/parsnip/tree/ordered), and an extension with engines is underway [here](https://github.com/corybrunson/ordered).

First see [this article](https://www.tidymodels.org/learn/develop/models/) for guidance on adding a new model.

### Checklist for adding a new model

Copied from [this article](https://parsnip.tidymodels.org/articles/checklists.html):

* [x] Create the main modeling function (e.g. `nearest_neighbors()`). When choosing argument names, check for existing ones across other model types which could be reused, e.g., `trees` for the number of trees is used across different tree-based models like `rand_forest()` and `boost_tree()`.
  - [here](https://github.com/corybrunson/parsnip/blob/59fe7023c77474127b9c1fab1512a3fd3f57ce79/R/ordinal_reg.R#L49)
  - Model parameters currently include `penalty`, `mixture`, `ordinal_link`, and `odds_link`.

* [x] Register the model and a mode in the parsnip model “database” with `parsnip::set_new_model()` and `parsnip::set_model_mode()`. [[example]](https://github.com/tidymodels/parsnip/blob/c54f07b7e1f7ce164aab8f95bc7b1356b68558c8/R/proportional_hazards_data.R)
  - [specification only](https://github.com/corybrunson/parsnip/blob/ordered/R/ordinal_reg_data.R)

* [x] Create an `update()` method.
  - [here](https://github.com/corybrunson/parsnip/blob/59fe7023c77474127b9c1fab1512a3fd3f57ce79/R/ordinal_reg.R#L84)

* [x] Add parameter objects for main parameters to *dials*, if needed. See [How to create a tuning parameter function](https://www.tidymodels.org/learn/develop/parameters/) for more details.
  - [here](https://github.com/corybrunson/dials/blob/ordered/R/param_ordinal_link.R)
  - This is done in [a coordinated fork branch](https://github.com/corybrunson/dials/tree/ordered).

* [x] Write unit tests for the basic modeling function (independent of the engines). 

* [x] Add a pkgdown entry.

* [x] Add model description to the internal `model_descs` tibble.

* [x] Run `purrr::map(parsnip:::extensions(), ~ library(.x, character.only = TRUE))`.

* [ ] Run `parsnip:::update_model_info_file()`.

* [ ] Make sure that no entries are removed from `inst/models.tsv`.

* [x] Add a documentation entry in `NEWS.md`.

title: harmonize penalty path control for elastic net `ordinal_reg` engines
description:
As originally implemented for the `ordinalNet` engine, and as adapted to the `glmnetcr` engine, when the user does not explicitly provide `path_values`, `translate()` silently modifies certain engine arguments in order to produce a penalty path with greater range and resolution than would be created by default:

``` r
library(parsnip)

# `glmnet`: `family` specified, others placeheld
glmnet_spec <- linear_reg(penalty = .01) |> 
  set_engine("glmnet")
( glmnet_tran <- translate(glmnet_spec) )
#> Linear Regression Model Specification (regression)
#> 
#> Main Arguments:
#>   penalty = 0.01
#> 
#> Computational engine: glmnet 
#> 
#> Model fit template:
#> glmnet::glmnet(x = missing_arg(), y = missing_arg(), weights = missing_arg(), 
#>     family = "gaussian")
print(glmnet_tran$method$fit$args)
#> $x
#> missing_arg()
#> 
#> $y
#> missing_arg()
#> 
#> $weights
#> missing_arg()
#> 
#> $family
#> [1] "gaussian"

# `ordinalNet`: translation silently modifies arguments for penalty path
ordinalNet_spec <- ordinal_reg(penalty = .01) |> 
  set_engine("ordinalNet")
( ordinalNet_tran <- translate(ordinalNet_spec) )
#> ! parsnip could not locate an implementation for `ordinal_reg` model
#>   specifications using the `ordinalNet` engine.
#> ℹ The parsnip extension package ordered implements support for this
#>   specification.
#> ℹ Please install (if needed) and load to continue.
#> Ordinal Regression Model Specification (classification)
#> 
#> Main Arguments:
#>   penalty = 0.01
#> 
#> Computational engine: ordinalNet
print(ordinalNet_tran$method$fit$args)
#> $nLambda
#> [1] 120
#> 
#> $lambdaMinRatio
#> [1] 1e-08
#> 
#> $includeLambda0
#> [1] TRUE

# `glmnetcr`: similar to `ordinalNet`
glmnetcr_spec <- ordinal_reg(penalty = .01) |> 
  set_engine("glmnetcr")
( glmnetcr_tran <- translate(glmnetcr_spec) )
#> ! parsnip could not locate an implementation for `ordinal_reg` model
#>   specifications using the `glmnetcr` engine.
#> ℹ The parsnip extension package ordered implements support for this
#>   specification.
#> ℹ Please install (if needed) and load to continue.
#> Ordinal Regression Model Specification (classification)
#> 
#> Main Arguments:
#>   penalty = 0.01
#> 
#> Computational engine: glmnetcr
print(glmnetcr_tran$method$fit$args)
#> $nlambda
#> [1] 120
#> 
#> $lambda.min.ratio
#> [1] 1e-08
```

<sup>Created on 2026-09-08 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

This was my design choice, and i now think it should be simplified, either to specify these values in `set_fit()` or not to intervene at all. The two major reasons are (1) that it violates parsnip norms so may be difficult for even proficient users to diagnose and (2) that it is different than the behavior of the `glmnet` engine.

Note that ordered intervenes also on prediction by using path endpoints rather than throwing an error (as `ordinalNet:::predict.ordinalNet()` does). I think this intervention should stay.

A draft revision is [here](https://github.com/corybrunson/parsnip/pull/2).

title: test-sparsevctrs.R glmnet mock fails in a full test run (S3 dispatch cache)
description:
`test-sparsevctrs.R`'s test `"we don't run as.matrix() on sparse matrix for glmnet pred #1210"` passes when the file is run on its own but fails in a full `devtools::test()` run:

```
Failure ('test-sparsevctrs.R:383:3'): we don't run as.matrix() on sparse matrix for glmnet pred #1210
Expected `predict(lm_fit, hotel_data)` to throw a error.
```

Reproduces with just two files:

```r
devtools::test(filter = "^(glmnet-engines|sparsevctrs)")   # 1 failure
devtools::test(filter = "^sparsevctrs")                    # 30 pass
```

`R CMD check` is unaffected, because it runs the tests against the installed package. That is why the failure has gone unnoticed.

## Cause

The test mocks glmnet's prediction method:

```r
local_mocked_bindings(
  predict.elnet = function(object, newx, ...) { ... },
  .package = "glmnet"
)
```

Once `predict.elnet` has been dispatched for real, R caches the resolved method. `local_mocked_bindings()` replaces the namespace binding, but dispatch keeps using the cached original:

```
real prediction done (predict.elnet now dispatched + cached)
getS3method sees mock: TRUE
result: dispatch used the ORIGINAL
```

`getS3method()` reports the mock while `UseMethod()` ignores it, which makes this awkward to diagnose. There is no supported way to invalidate that cache from the test, so the mock cannot be made reliable.

Bisecting the preceding file confirms the mechanism. `test-glmnet-engines.R` has three blocks: the first only *fits* glmnet models and is harmless, while the second and third make glmnet *predictions* and each trigger the failure.

This is the hazard the contributing guidance warns about for the `.package` argument to `local_mocked_bindings()`.

## Suggested fix

No mock is needed. parsnip already owns the decision point this test is about: `organize_glmnet_pre_pred()` (`R/glmnet-engines.R`) builds the `newx` that glmnet receives, returning the matrix untouched when it is sparse and calling `as.matrix()` otherwise. Testing that function directly covers the #1210 invariant, with no namespace modification and no ordering assumptions:

- a sparse input stays sparse, with columns subset to the fitted coefficients
- a dense input stays a dense matrix
- the registered prediction module really does route `newx` through it, asserted against `get_from_env("linear_reg_predict")`, so the unit test cannot pass while the wiring is broken
- `predict()` on sparse data still runs without error

## Origin

Introduced by `test-glmnet-engines.R`, added in #1436 for #857 and #878. The test file itself is fine; it simply makes a glmnet prediction earlier in the run than `test-sparsevctrs.R`, which is enough to defeat the mock.

title: Suggest offset() in the formula when offset is passed to fit()
description:
Since #492, `fit()` errors when anything is passed through `...`. For `offset` specifically, the generic message points users somewhere that only half works:

```r
library(parsnip)
linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm") |>
  fit(mpg ~ wt + cyl, offset = am, data = mtcars)
#> Error in `fit()`:
#> ! `...` must be empty.
#> x Problematic argument: `offset`.
#> i Arguments for the model fit should be passed to `set_engine()`, and case
#>   weights to the `case_weights` argument.
```

Following that advice literally does not work:

```r
linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm", offset = am) |>
  fit(mpg ~ wt + cyl, data = mtcars)
#> Error: invalid type (language) for variable '(offset)'
```

The bare symbol is never evaluated against `data`, so the user gets a second, more cryptic error. It only works if the vector is fully qualified:

```r
linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm", offset = mtcars$am) |>
  fit(mpg ~ wt + cyl, data = mtcars)   # works
```

## Suggestion

When `offset` appears in `...`, add a bullet to the existing error recommending `offset()` in the formula:

```r
fit(mpg ~ wt + cyl + offset(am), data = mtcars)
```

That is the standard R idiom, it evaluates in `data`, and it avoids the bare-symbol trap entirely.

Verified that it genuinely applies the offset for every formula-interface engine tried — `linear_reg()` with `"lm"` and `"glm"`, and `logistic_reg()` with `"glm"` — and, perhaps less obviously, for glmnet as well, even though parsnip converts the formula to x/y for that engine:

```r
d <- transform(mtcars, lo = log(wt))
linear_reg(penalty = 0.1) |>
  set_engine("glmnet") |>
  fit(mpg ~ wt + cyl + offset(lo), data = d)   # offset stored on the fit
```

So a single recommendation covers all of them, which keeps the message simple.

## Scope

Nine model/engine combinations currently have an `offset` formal, so this is not limited to `lm`:

`gen_additive_mod`/mgcv, `linear_reg`/lm, `linear_reg`/glm, `linear_reg`/glmnet, `linear_reg`/stan, `logistic_reg`/glm, `logistic_reg`/glmnet, `logistic_reg`/stan, `multinom_reg`/glmnet

The check lives in `check_fit_dots()` (`R/fit.R`), which runs before engine dispatch, so the extra bullet would be keyed on the argument name rather than being engine-aware. That seems fine given the formula idiom works across all the engines above.

## Why this came up

parsnip's reverse-dependency check for the current dev version reported one new problem: tidypredict's `lm.Rmd` vignette, which calls `fit(..., offset = am)`. Worth noting that the offset was never actually applied there — before #492 the dots were silently dropped on the formula-to-formula path, and the coefficients are byte-identical to `lm(mpg ~ wt + cyl)` with no offset. #492 did not change the model, it exposed that the example had never worked. A clearer error would have made that much faster to diagnose.

title: Remove `predict_<type>_glmnet()` for all types but `"raw"`
description: Following on from #877, the glmnet methods for `predict_numeric()`, `predict_class()`, and `predict_classprob()` would only evaluate the model spec before handing off to the method for `model_fit`. Let's check if that is necessary or if we can remove those functions altogether.

title: Disable `type = "raw"` for `multi_predict()`
description:
This is an example for glmnet but this should probably apply to all models/engines.

For glmnet, `multi_predict()` currently ignores `type = "raw"` when applied to a linear regression, but errors (in glmnet) for logistic and multinomial regression.

``` r
library(parsnip)

data("hpc_data", package = "modeldata")
hpc <- hpc_data[1:150, c(2:5, 8)]
lm_spec <- linear_reg(penalty = 0.123) |> set_engine("glmnet")
lm_fit <- fit(lm_spec, input_fields ~ log(compounds) + class, data = hpc)
multi_predict(lm_fit, hpc[1:5,], type = "raw", penalty = c(0.1, 0.5)) 
#> # A tibble: 5 × 1
#>   .pred           
#>   <list>          
#> 1 <tibble [2 × 2]>
#> 2 <tibble [2 × 2]>
#> 3 <tibble [2 × 2]>
#> 4 <tibble [2 × 2]>
#> 5 <tibble [2 × 2]>

data("lending_club", package = "modeldata")
lending_club <- lending_club[1:200, ]
lr_spec <- logistic_reg(penalty = 0.123) |> set_engine("glmnet")
lr_fit <- fit(lr_spec, Class ~ log(funded_amnt) + int_rate + term, data = lending_club)
multi_predict(lr_fit, lending_club[1:5,], type = "raw", penalty = c(0.123, 0.5))
#> Error in match.arg(type): 'arg' should be one of "link", "response", "coefficients", "class", "nonzero"
```

title: Disable `...` for `fit()`
description:
Currently, the documentation for `fit()` says for `...`

> Not currently used; values passed here will be ignored. Other options required to fit the model should be passed using `set_engine()`.

However, some arguments get passed through in some cases, see examples below. Any additional arguments should be specified via `set_engine()` and `fit()` should error informatively if the dots are used.

Current status:
* formula to formula: fails silently
* formula to xy: allowed args are `c("subset", "weights", "contrasts", "offset")`
* xy to xy: fails in `eval_mod()`

``` r
library(parsnip)

fit_parsnip$fit %>% fitted() %>% length()
```

title: `xy_xy()` sets `y_var` to `character(0)` for Surv objects
description:
`fit_xy()` correctly extracts `y_var` from the outcome at 

https://github.com/tidymodels/parsnip/blob/509ffdfd9d31d4625da249d3ce54ad7cd5d9bb6e/R/fit.R#L284

and stores it in `eval_env$y_var` at

https://github.com/tidymodels/parsnip/blob/509ffdfd9d31d4625da249d3ce54ad7cd5d9bb6e/R/fit.R#L300

However, `xy_xy()` in `fit_helpers.R` ignores `env$y_var` and re-derives it using an `is.atomic()` check:

https://github.com/tidymodels/parsnip/blob/509ffdfd9d31d4625da249d3ce54ad7cd5d9bb6e/R/fit_helpers.R#L122-L127

`Surv` objects are atomic (`is.atomic(Surv(...))` returns `TRUE`), so `y_var` is incorrectly set to `character(0)`.

The sibling function `xy_form()` already handles this correctly (lines 211–212):

https://github.com/tidymodels/parsnip/blob/509ffdfd9d31d4625da249d3ce54ad7cd5d9bb6e/R/fit_helpers.R#L211-L219

This bug is not currently triggered in practice because all censored regression engines use formula interfaces (routing through `xy_form()`). It would become a problem if a censored regression engine with a matrix or data.frame interface is added.

## Fix

Apply the same pattern from `xy_form()` to `xy_xy()` — use `env$y_var` when available:

```r
if (!is.null(env$y_var)) {

  y_name <- env$y_var
} else if (is.atomic(env$y)) {
  y_name <- character(0)
} else {
  y_name <- colnames(env$y)
}
res$preproc <- list(y_var = y_name, x_names = colnames(env$x))
```

## Reprex

```r
library(survival)

s <- Surv(1:5, c(1, 0, 1, 1, 0))
is.atomic(s)
#> [1] TRUE
colnames(s)
#> [1] "time" "status"
```

No user-facing reprex is possible today because no censored regression engine uses the `xy_xy()` path, but the inconsistency between the two helpers should be resolved.

title: `multi_predict()` for kknn errors when `neighbors` isn't supplied
description:
In `R/nearest_neighbor.R`, `multi_predict._train.kknn()` falls back to the fitted call's `ks` value when `neighbors` is not supplied:

```r
multi_predict._train.kknn <-
  function(object, new_data, type = NULL, neighbors = NULL, ...) {
    if (is.null(neighbors)) {
      neighbors <- rlang::eval_tidy(object$fit$call$ks)
    }
    neighbors <- sort(neighbors)
    ...
```

`object$fit$call$ks` holds the *unevaluated call expression* used to fit the model, not the actual fitted `k` value. Evaluating it with `rlang::eval_tidy()` here re-executes that stale call outside of its original environment, which errors or produces the wrong value instead of the number of neighbors the model was actually fit with.

reprex:
``` r
library(parsnip)
fit <- nearest_neighbor(neighbors = 7) |>
  set_engine("kknn") |>
  set_mode("regression") |>
  fit(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars)
multi_predict(fit, new_data = mtcars[1:3, ])
#> Error in `if (num_rows > n - offset) ...`:
#> ! argument is of length zero
```

<sup>Created on 2026-08-31 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

Suggested fix: read the actual fitted `k` (e.g. `object$fit$best.parameters$k` or similar accessor) instead of re-evaluating `object$fit$call$ks`.

title: `multi_predict_args.workflow()` returns a `model_fit`/workflow object instead of argument names
description:
In `R/aaa_multi_predict.R`:

```r
#' @export
#' @rdname has_multi_predict
multi_predict_args.workflow <- function(object, ...) {
  object <- object$fit$model$model
}
```

This method is supposed to return the character vector of argument names supporting submodel prediction (as `multi_predict_args.model_fit()` does), but instead it just extracts the fitted model object from the workflow and returns *that*, without ever calling into `multi_predict_args()`. Callers expecting a character vector get a `model_fit` object instead, which breaks any code checking `has_multi_predict()`/`multi_predict_args()` on workflows.

reprex:
``` r
library(parsnip)
library(workflows)
wf <- workflow() |>
  add_formula(mpg ~ .) |>
  add_model(nearest_neighbor(neighbors = 7) |> set_engine("kknn") |> set_mode("regression"))
wf_fit <- fit(wf, data = mtcars)
multi_predict_args(wf_fit)
str(wf_fit$fit$model$model)
#>  NULL
```

<sup>Created on 2026-08-31 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

On the currently installed workflows version, `object$fit$model$model` doesn't even exist any more (the fitted model now lives at `object$fit$fit`), so the method returns bare `NULL` instead of `"neighbors"` — an even more silent failure than originally described.

Suggested fix: `multi_predict_args.workflow <- function(object, ...) { multi_predict_args(object$fit$fit, ...) }`, recursing into the extracted model fit rather than returning it directly.

title: `predict_raw()` errors whenever `opts` contains a protected argument name
description:
In `R/predict_raw.R`:

```r
predict_raw.model_fit <- function(object, new_data, opts = list(), ...) {
  protected_args <- names(object$spec$method$pred$raw$args)
  dup_args <- names(opts) %in% protected_args
  if (any(dup_args)) {
    opts <- opts[[!dup_args]]
  }
  ...
```

`dup_args` is a logical vector, but `opts[[!dup_args]]` uses double-bracket indexing, which requires a single scalar index, not a logical vector. This throws an error any time a user passes an `opts` argument whose name overlaps with a protected prediction argument, instead of silently dropping the duplicate as intended.

reprex:
``` r
library(parsnip)
fit <- linear_reg() |> set_engine("lm") |> fit(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars)
predict_raw(fit, mtcars, opts = list(newdata = mtcars))
#> Error in `opts[[!dup_args]]`:
#> ! attempt to select less than one element in integerOneIndex
```

<sup>Created on 2026-08-31 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

(Using `opts = list(newdata = mtcars)`, which actually collides with a protected argument name, to trigger the bug — `opts = list(type = ...)` doesn't overlap any protected arg for the `lm` engine so it doesn't hit the buggy branch.)

Suggested fix: change `opts[[!dup_args]]` to `opts[!dup_args]` (single-bracket subsetting, which correctly handles a logical vector).

title: Setting `relax = TRUE` for glmnet models fails
description:
Following on from https://github.com/tidymodels/poissonreg/issues/82: 

This affects all glmnet models we wrap in tidymodels (not just here in poissonreg) where we set `relax = TRUE`. Here is an example with `linear_reg()` and main arguments and engine arguments, respectively.

``` r
library(parsnip)

mod <- linear_reg(penalty = 0.5, mixture = 1) %>%
  set_engine("glmnet", relax = TRUE) %>% 
  fit(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars)
#> Error in `glmnet::glmnet()`:
#> ! Base operators are not defined for quosures. Do you need to unquote
#>   the quosure?
#> 
#> # Bad: myquosure > rhs
#> 
#> # Good: !!myquosure > rhs


mod <- linear_reg(penalty = 0.5) %>%
  set_engine("glmnet", relax = TRUE, maxit = 1000) %>% 
  fit(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars)
#> Warning: from glmnet C++ code (error code -63); Convergence for 63th lambda
#> value not reached after maxit=1000 iterations; solutions for larger lambdas
#> returned
#> Error in elnet(xd, is.sparse, y, weights, offset, type.gaussian, alpha, : 'language' object cannot be coerced to type 'integer'
```

<sup>Created on 2024-02-16 with [reprex v2.1.0](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

This is because `glmnet::glmnet()` calls `glmnet::relax.glmnet()` with the "regular" fit object ([glmnet code snippet](https://github.com/cran/glmnet/blob/625f6ca6e3132ce730563ce34233c37f347754c8/R/glmnet.R#L530-L533)).

`glmnet::relax.glmnet()` uses that `fit` object to [refit without any regularization](https://glmnet.stanford.edu/reference/glmnet.html) .  That happens via `stats::update.default()` ([glmnet code snippet](https://github.com/cran/glmnet/blob/625f6ca6e3132ce730563ce34233c37f347754c8/R/relax.glmnet.R#L66)) which uses `eval()` to evaluate the `call` -- but that `call` contains the arguments as quosures. That is what ultimately breaks `eval()`.

title: Remove data descriptors (.cols(), .lvls(), .obs(), ...)
description:
Data descriptors — `.cols()`, `.preds()`, `.obs()`, `.lvls()`, `.facts()`, `.x()`, `.y()`, `.dat()` — let a model specification refer to properties of the training data that are only known at fit time:

```r
rand_forest(mode = "classification", mtry = .cols() - 2)
```

Supporting them is the main reason model and engine arguments are held as quosures all the way to the fit call, and that laziness has a real cost.

## Why remove them

Leaving arguments unevaluated until the engine forces them is what leaks raw quosures into the call an engine records. Engines that re-evaluate their own recorded call with base `eval()` then fail, because base `eval()` cannot handle a quosure. Two long-standing bugs had this single root cause:

- #432 — `mars()` with `prune_method = "cv"` and `prod_degree`; earth's cv path re-dispatches through `update.earth()`.
- #1069 — `set_engine("glmnet", relax = TRUE)`; `relax.glmnet()` refits through `stats::update.default()`. This also affected the poissonreg and censored wrappers.

Both are now fixed by evaluating quosure arguments while the fit call is assembled, so **this issue is no longer blocking either of them**. What remains is the simplification that removal would unlock.

Machinery that exists wholly or largely to accommodate descriptors:

- `maybe_eval()` (`R/arguments.R:150-158`) wraps evaluation in `try()` and silently falls back to the unevaluated quosure, specifically because "if descriptors are in `x`, eval fails". That fallback now hides genuine evaluation errors and could become a plain `eval_tidy()`.
- The quosure-evaluation loop in `multi_predict._earth()` (`R/mars.R:159-167`) and the equivalent cleanup in `repair_call()` exist to undo the same problem after the fact.
- `requires_descrs()`, `has_any_descrs()`, `is_descr()`, `poke_descrs()`, `scoped_descrs()`, `get_descr_form()`, `get_descr_xy()`, `get_descr_df()`, `get_descr_spark()` and the `descr_env` mutable environment.

## Footprint

Smaller than it looks. The machinery is well isolated:

| | |
|---|---|
| `R/descriptors.R` | 432 lines |
| `tests/testthat/test-descriptors.R` | 237 lines |
| Exported functions | 8 (`.cols`, `.preds`, `.obs`, `.lvls`, `.facts`, `.x`, `.y`, `.dat`) |
| Call sites outside `R/descriptors.R` | 2, both in `R/fit_helpers.R` (lines 38-40 and 101-103) |
| Documentation | `man/descriptors.Rd`, plus references in `R/model_object_docs.R:117-121` and `:216` |

Only one test in the rest of the suite depends on descriptor behaviour: `test-rand_forest_ranger.R`'s "additional descriptor tests", which fits ranger with `class.weights = c(min(.lvls()), 20, 10, 1)`.

## Suggested sequence

1. Run reverse-dependency checks against a branch with descriptors disabled, to find any package that uses them in practice. (topepo is doing this.)
2. Depending on the result, either deprecate the eight functions with `lifecycle` and make them defunct on the normal schedule, or remove them outright if nothing downstream uses them.
3. Remove `descr_env` and the `poke`/`scoped` machinery, and drop the two `requires_descrs()` branches in `R/fit_helpers.R`.
4. Simplify `maybe_eval()` to a plain `eval_tidy()`, and drop the now-redundant quosure cleanups in `multi_predict._earth()` and `repair_call()`.
5. Update `man/descriptors.Rd` and the `model_object_docs.R` references.

One thing to decide during step 2: whether any part of `.x()`, `.y()` and `.dat()` should survive in some other form. They return the training data itself rather than a summary statistic, so they are a different kind of thing from `.cols()` and `.obs()` and may have different downstream usage.

## Note on failure mode

Whatever the mechanism, the descriptors should fail loudly rather than silently. With `maybe_eval()`'s current `try()` fallback in place, a descriptor that errors is silently replaced by the unevaluated quosure and then passed to the engine, which produces a confusing downstream error instead of a clear one. Any disable or deprecation step needs that fallback addressed at the same time, or the intended message never reaches the user.

title: BART classification prediction interval bounds scrambled across observations
description:
In `R/bart.R`, when computing classification `conf_int`/`pred_int` bounds:

```r
bnds <- apply(post_dist, 2, quantile, probs = c(lo, hi), na.rm = TRUE)
bnds <- apply(bnds, 1, function(x) sort(x))
```

`bnds` from the first `apply()` is a 2-row matrix (rows = the lo/hi quantiles, columns = observations). The second `apply(bnds, 1, sort)` sorts *across observations within each quantile row*, rather than sorting the lo/hi pair *within each observation (column)*. This mixes quantile values from different observations, so `.pred_lower_*`/`.pred_upper_*` for a given row can come from an entirely different observation's posterior distribution.

reprex:
``` r
library(parsnip)
set.seed(1)
fit <- bart(trees = 5) |> set_engine("dbarts") |> set_mode("classification") |>
  fit(Species ~ ., data = iris[iris$Species != "virginica", ])
predict(fit, iris[1:5, ], type = "conf_int")
#> Error in `rlang::set_names()`:
#> ! The size of `nm` (6) must be compatible with the size of `x` (4).
```

<sup>Created on 2026-08-31 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

On the currently installed dbarts/parsnip versions this surfaces as an outright error rather than silently wrong numbers, because `apply(bnds, 1, sort)` also changes the shape of the result. Either way, the fix is the same.

Suggested fix: sort within each column, e.g. `bnds <- apply(bnds, 2, sort)` (transposed appropriately), so lo/hi are reordered per-observation rather than per-quantile-across-observations.

title: XGBoost Monotone Constraint Factor Levels Reversed
description:
## The problem

Hey @juliasilge and @topepo et. al! 

**First**: I'm not 100% sure this is a bug, but it was unexpected behavior so I figured I'd file this. 

The TL;DR is that it appears that `parsnip` is happy to take a factor as a response variable, accept monotone constraints, and then do whatever it needs to do to convert that factor into a numeric matrix for XGBoost and thread the constraints through. But we stumbled upon some unexpected behavior: When we have the equivalent of `event_level = "second"` and want to set a positive monotone constraint on one of our features (i.e. "An increase in X is associated with an increase in the log-odds of `Y == TRUE`"), we end up with the reverse behavior we'd expect. See `reprex` below. My suspicion is that this just has to do with XGBoost itself assuming that the "true" class is the first level in the factor, but I'm not sure. 

Regardless, I expect this is an XGB issue and not a `parsnip` issue per se, but it'd be nice to warn the user if they pass constraints like this to check their factor levels.

## Reproducible example
``` r
library(tidymodels)
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(14159)

d <- iris %>%
  filter(
    Species %in% c("setosa", "virginica")
  ) %>%
  transmute(
    id = 1:n(),
    sepal_length = Sepal.Length,
    is_virginica = ifelse(Species == "virginica", "yes", "no")
  ) %>%
  tibble()

d
#> # A tibble: 100 × 3
#>       id sepal_length is_virginica
#>    <int>        <dbl> <chr>       
#>  1     1          5.1 no          
#>  2     2          4.9 no          
#>  3     3          4.7 no          
#>  4     4          4.6 no          
#>  5     5          5   no          
#>  6     6          5.4 no          
#>  7     7          4.6 no          
#>  8     8          5   no          
#>  9     9          4.4 no          
#> 10    10          4.9 no          
#> # … with 90 more rows
#> # ℹ Use `print(n = ...)` to see more rows

## Just to convince you that sepal_length should,
##  in fact, have a positive effect
d %>%
  ggplot() +
  aes(
    x = is_virginica,
    y = sepal_length,
    fill = is_virginica
  ) +
  geom_boxplot()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/HyrcHKI.png)

``` r

fit_predict <- function(dir) {
  constraint <- switch(
    dir,
    "up" = "(1)",
    "down" = "(-1)"
  )
  
  s <- boost_tree() %>%
    set_mode("classification") %>%
    set_engine(
      "xgboost",
      monotone_constraints = constraint
    )
  
  r <- recipe(
    is_virginica ~ sepal_length,
    data = d
  )
  
  w <- workflow() %>%
    add_model(s) %>%
    add_recipe(r)
  
  m <- fit(
    w,
    d
  )
  
  d %>%
    mutate(
      dir = dir,
      pred = predict(m, d, type = "prob")$.pred_yes
    )
}

predictions <- map_dfr(
  c("up", "down"),
  fit_predict
)

predictions %>%
  ggplot() +
  aes(
    x = sepal_length,
    y = pred,
    color = is_virginica,
    shape = dir
  ) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ dir,
    ncol = 2
  )
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/1XcfYke.png)

<sup>Created on 2022-08-18 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

title: print() on a bart() spec dispatches to dbarts::print.bart once the dbarts namespace is loaded
description:
Printing a `bart()` model specification breaks as soon as the dbarts namespace is loaded, because dbarts exports an S3 method `print.bart()` and parsnip's `bart()` spec has `"bart"` as its first class.

No `library(dbarts)` is needed — parsnip loads the namespace itself the first time you fit a BART model, so a pure-parsnip session breaks itself:

```r
library(parsnip)

spec <- bart(mode = "regression")
spec
#> BART Model Specification (regression)
#> 
#> Computational engine: dbarts

fit(spec, mpg ~ ., data = mtcars)   # loads the dbarts namespace

spec
#> 
#> Call:
#> NULL
```

Every `bart()` spec in the session prints as `Call: NULL` from then on.

## Root cause

`bart()` returns an object of class `c("bart", "model_spec")`:

```r
class(bart())
#> [1] "bart"       "model_spec"
```

dbarts registers `S3method(print, bart)` for its own fitted BART objects. That registration happens when the namespace is **loaded**, not attached, so `loadNamespace("dbarts")` alone is enough to redirect dispatch:

```r
library(parsnip)
spec <- parsnip::bart()
loadNamespace("dbarts")
"package:dbarts" %in% search()
#> [1] FALSE
spec
#> 
#> Call:
#> NULL
```

`print()` finds `dbarts:::print.bart` before it ever reaches `parsnip:::print.model_spec`. That method just does `cat("\nCall:\n", deparse(x$call), ...)`, and a `model_spec` has no `$call`, hence `NULL`.

## This is the mirror image of #600

In #600 (2021) the collision ran the other way: parsnip defined `print.bart()` and it hijacked dbarts' *fitted* objects, because dbarts had no print method at the time. That was resolved by parsnip dropping its method. dbarts has since added one (present in 0.9.33), so the same class-name collision now bites in the opposite direction.

Worth keeping in mind when picking a fix: re-adding `print.bart()` to parsnip would recreate #600 unless it explicitly falls through to dbarts for non-`model_spec` objects. `"bart"` is the only parsnip model-type name that collides with an S3 method in its own engine package — I scanned every installed package's S3 method table against every registered parsnip model type, and the only other hits are `stats::update.*` and `stats::predict.mars`-style false positives that never win dispatch.

## Effect on the test suite

`test-model_basics.R:6:3` fails in a full `devtools::test()` run:

```
── 1. Failure ('test-model_basics.R:6:3'): basic object classes and print method
Snapshot of code has changed:
    old                                       | new                
[1] Code                                      | Code            [1]
[2]   print(bart())                           |   print(bart()) [2]
[3] Output                                    | Output          [3]
[4]   BART Model Specification (unknown mode) -                 [4]
[5]                                           -   Call:         [5]
[6]   Computational engine: dbarts            -   NULL          [6]
```

It passes when that file runs on its own. Test files run alphabetically, so `test-bart.R` fits BART models and loads the dbarts namespace before `test-model_basics.R` prints the spec. This looks like test pollution but it is reporting a real user-facing bug.

## Session info

- parsnip 1.6.0.9001 (`main`, 8ca7373e)
- dbarts 0.9.33
- R 4.6.1

title: earth multiclass classification predictions use binary threshold rule, giving wrong classes
description:
In `R/mars_data.R`, the `"class"` prediction post-processor for the earth engine is hardcoded for binary classification:

```r
set_pred(
  model = "mars",
  eng = "earth",
  mode = "classification",
  type = "class",
  value = list(
    pre = NULL,
    post = function(x, object) {
      x <- ifelse(x[, 1] >= 0.5, object$lvl[2], object$lvl[1])
      x
    },
    ...
```

This assumes `x` is a single-column probability vector thresholded at 0.5, which only makes sense for two-class outcomes. For a multiclass outcome, `earth`'s `predict(..., type = "response")` returns one column per class, and this logic silently returns incorrect classes since it only ever looks at column 1 against a fixed cutoff.

reprex:
``` r
library(parsnip)
fit <- mars(mode = "classification") |> set_engine("earth") |>
  fit(Species ~ ., data = iris)
#> Warning: glm.fit: algorithm did not converge
#> Warning: glm.fit: fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred
#> Warning: glm.fit: fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred
#> Warning: glm.fit: fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred
#> Warning: the glm algorithm did not converge for response "setosa"
predict(fit, iris, type = "class")
#> # A tibble: 150 × 1
#>    .pred_class
#>    <fct>      
#>  1 versicolor 
#>  2 versicolor 
#>  3 versicolor 
#>  4 versicolor 
#>  5 versicolor 
#>  6 versicolor 
#>  7 versicolor 
#>  8 versicolor 
#>  9 versicolor 
#> 10 versicolor 
#> # ℹ 140 more rows
```

<sup>Created on 2026-08-31 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

Every one of the 150 rows is predicted as `versicolor`, regardless of the true species — the binary threshold rule collapses the 3-class problem into a single always-predicted class.

Suggested fix: branch on `length(object$lvl)`: for 2 classes keep the current threshold logic, for >2 classes take `object$lvl[apply(x, 1, which.max)]`.

title: Support for multi-level outcomes in MARS classification
description:
## Multi-level outcomes in MARS classification

Looking at the code in `mars_data.R`, it appears that only binary classification prediction is currently supported. 

```r
set_pred(
  model = "mars",
  eng = "earth",
  mode = "classification",
  type = "class",
  value = list(
    pre = NULL,
    post = function(x, object) {
      x <- ifelse(x[, 1] >= 0.5, object$lvl[2], object$lvl[1])
      x
    },
    func = c(fun = "predict"),
    args =
      list(
        object = quote(object$fit),
        newdata = quote(new_data),
        type = "response"
      )
  )
)

set_pred(
  model = "mars",
  eng = "earth",
  mode = "classification",
  type = "prob",
  value = list(
    pre = NULL,
    post = function(x, object) {
      x <- x[, 1]
      x <- tibble(v1 = 1 - x, v2 = x)
      colnames(x) <- object$lvl
      x
    },
    func = c(fun = "predict"),
    args =
      list(
        object = quote(object$fit),
        newdata = quote(new_data),
        type = "response"
      )
  )
)

```

title: svm_linear() LiblineaR regression prediction test fails with LiblineaR 2.10-25
description:
CRAN released LiblineaR 2.10-25, which changed the numeric output of the L2-regularized L2-loss linear SVM regression solver used by \`svm_linear(engine = "LiblineaR")\`.

This broke the hardcoded expected values in \`test-svm_linear.R\`'s \`'linear svm regression prediction: LiblineaR'\` test, causing \`test-coverage\` CI to fail (see PR #1414).

Locally reproduced with LiblineaR 2.10-25:

\`\`\`
  `actual$.pred`:  85.1 576.2 1886.1
`expected$.pred`: 117.0 593.0 1862.9
\`\`\`

The test has been temporarily skipped (\`skip("fix this later")\`) in that PR. We need to determine whether this is:

- an intentional algorithm change in LiblineaR 2.10-25 (in which case the hardcoded expected values in the test should just be updated), or
- a regression/bug in LiblineaR worth reporting upstream.

Once resolved, remove the \`skip()\` and update the expected values in \`tests/testthat/test-svm_linear.R\`.

title: LiblineaR update breakage
description:
From the maintainer: 

> Version 2.10-25 of the R package LiblineaR, submitted today, still mirrors version 2.10 of LIBLINEAR but sees its tests suite deeply improved, as well as a handful of bugs fixed. 
> 
> Namely, this new version fixes a bug where LiblineaR()'s epsilon (solver convergence tolerance) silently defaulted to 0.01 for every solver type, rather than LIBLINEAR's own documented per-solver default. That's now corrected.
> 
> Your svm_linear() LiblineaR regression engine in parsnip uses type=11 without setting epsilon explicitly, so it now converges under LIBLINEAR's real default for that solver (0.001) instead of the old, incorrect 0.01. On the hpc dataset used in tests/testthat/test-svm_linear.R, this produces a materially different (not just numerically-noisier) fit, so the hardcoded expected values in liblinear_pred (around line 104) and the corresponding xy-form check (around line 123) no longer match within the tolerance = 0.0001 used there.
> 
> CRAN's reverse-dependency pretest for our submission caught this and flagged it as a "change to worse".

title: LiblineaR `cost` parameter mapped to wrong argument name, silently ignored during tuning
description:
In `R/svm_linear_data.R`, the `set_model_arg()` call for the LiblineaR engine maps parsnip's `cost` to the original argument `"C"`:

```r
set_model_arg(
  model = "svm_linear",
  eng = "LiblineaR",
  parsnip = "cost",
  original = "C",
  func = list(pkg = "dials", fun = "cost", range = c(-10, 5)),
  has_submodel = FALSE
)
```

However, `LiblineaR::LiblineaR()` names this argument `cost`, not `C`. Because `"C"` doesn't match any formal argument of `LiblineaR()`, the value silently fails to be passed through, and the model falls back to LiblineaR's internal default cost rather than the value specified by the user or a tuning grid.

reprex:
``` r
library(parsnip)
translate(svm_linear(cost = 1) |> set_engine("LiblineaR") |> set_mode("classification"))
#> Linear Support Vector Machine Model Specification (classification)
#> 
#> Main Arguments:
#>   cost = 1
#> 
#> Computational engine: LiblineaR 
#> 
#> Model fit template:
#> LiblineaR::LiblineaR(x = missing_arg(), y = missing_arg(), C = 1, 
#>     type = 1)
```

<sup>Created on 2026-08-31 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

Note the fit template passes `C = 1` to `LiblineaR()`, which has no `C` argument.

Suggested fix: change `original = "C"` to `original = "cost"`.

title: Move arg registration for `bag_tree()`'s `rpart` engine to parsnip from baguette
description:
This originally surfaced in censored but basically: baguette registers the model args for `bag_tree()` with the `rpart` engine. 

https://github.com/tidymodels/baguette/blob/237f2e6df0d8fdc24eed430db4abf3a88fe81f4d/R/bag_tree_data.R#L17-L50

censored also registered that model/engine combo, just for a different mode. So the arguments are only tunable for censored regression if we also load baguette, like we've encountered in extratests:

https://github.com/tidymodels/extratests/blob/307268a1aa4974a3a89248abbcf7d61adfac96c9/tests/testthat/test-censored-case-weights.R#L15-L16

So because both extension package register the same engine, just with a different mode, the shared part of that registration (i.e. things that are not mode-specific) should go into parsnip.

---

The `bag_tree()` rpart engine for censored regression registers no model
arguments, so none of `bag_tree()`'s main args (`cost_complexity`,
`tree_depth`, `min_n`, `class_cost`) are tunable. `extract_parameter_set_dials()`
and `tunable()` both come back empty, which means a bagged survival tree cannot
be tuned at all. Every other tree-based censored engine surfaces at least its
tree-control main args, so this looks like a gap rather than a deliberate
choice.

## Reproducible example

``` r
library(censored)
#> Loading required package: parsnip
#> Loading required package: survival

# All of bag_tree()'s main args, set to tune(), for the rpart engine
spec <- bag_tree(
  cost_complexity = tune(),
  tree_depth = tune(),
  min_n = tune()
) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("censored regression")

# No tuning parameters are surfaced
hardhat::extract_parameter_set_dials(spec)
#> Collection of 0 parameters for tuning
#> 
#> [1] identifier type       object    
#> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)
#> 

# tunable() confirms the rpart engine registers none
generics::tunable(spec)
#> # A tibble: 0 × 5
#> # ℹ 5 variables: name <chr>, call_info <list>, source <chr>, component <chr>,
#> #   component_id <chr>
```

## Expected behaviour

The tree-control main args that `ipred::bagging()` passes through to the
underlying `rpart` fit (`cost_complexity` → `cp`, `tree_depth` → `maxdepth`,
`min_n` → `minsplit`) should be registered via `set_model_arg()` in
`R/bag_tree-data.R` so they are tunable, mirroring `decision_tree()` with rpart.

title: Per-mode differences in sparsity encoding not respected
description:
The `ranger` engines for regression and classification use the data frame interface to `ranger::ranger()` and allow sparsity in the parsnip encodings. The `ranger` engine for censored regression (https://github.com/tidymodels/censored/pull/376) uses the formula interface and thus doesn't allow sparsity. Encodings are register for a combination of model-engine-mode so those _should_ not clash. It surfaced in https://github.com/tidymodels/extratests/pull/301

``` r
library(tidymodels)

data("ames", package = "modeldata")

rec_spec <- recipe(Sale_Price ~ ., data = ames) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors(), sparse = "yes")

mod_spec <- rand_forest("regression", "ranger")

wf_spec <- workflow(rec_spec, mod_spec)

options("sparsevctrs.verbose_materialize" = 2)

testthat::expect_no_warning(
  wf_fit <- fit(wf_spec, ames)
)

library(censored)
#> Loading required package: survival

testthat::expect_no_warning(
  wf_fit <- fit(wf_spec, ames)
)
#> Error:
#> ! Expected `wf_fit <- fit(wf_spec, ames)` not to throw any warnings.
#> Actually got a <rlang_warning> with message:
#>   `x` is a sparse tibble, but `rand_forest()` with engine "ranger" doesn't accept
#>   that. Converting to non-sparse.
```

title: Outdated Brier Score Formulation
description:
Yardstick uses the version from Assessment and Comparison of Prognostic Classification Schemes for Survival Data, _Statistics in Medicine_, 1999. However, there is Consistent Estimation of the Expected Brier Score in General Survival Models with Right-Censored Event Times, _Biometrical Journal_, 2006.

> Graf et al. (1999) proposed estimators of the expected Brier score that avoid any dependence on the assumed survival model. The latter work describes carefully the censoring bias but excludes a careful analysis of the proposed estimator. Unlike Graf et al. (1999), we clearly distinguish the mean squared error from the expected mean squared error. As a by-product we obtain a direct correspondence between the expected Brier score and the measure proposed in Schemper and Henderson (2000). It turns out that a conditional weighting scheme improves on the marginal weighting scheme used in Graf et al. (1999) regarding uniform consistency.

The newer Brier score metric seems improved upon Graf (1999). This is related to tidymodels/yardstick#537.

title: `predict(type = "survival")` output lacks `.weight_censored` column required by `roc_auc_survival()`
description:
Hello,

`yardstick::roc_auc_survival()` requires survival-probability predictions that include a column named `.weight_censored`. `parsnip::augment()` adds this column automatically, but `predict(..., type = "survival")` returns only `.eval_time` and `.pred_survival`, which causes `roc_auc_survival()` to error.


``` r
library(dplyr)
library(parsnip)
library(yardstick)
library(survival)
library(censored)

lung$surv <- Surv(lung$time, lung$status)

# pipeline works well for concordance_survival
proportional_hazards() %>% 
  fit(surv ~ ph.ecog + age, data = lung) %>% 
  predict(lung, type = "time") %>% 
  bind_cols(lung) %>% 
  concordance_survival(surv, .pred_time)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>   .metric              .estimator .estimate
#>   <chr>                <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 concordance_survival standard       0.610

# error for roc_auc_survival
proportional_hazards() %>% 
  fit(surv ~ ph.ecog + age, data = lung) %>% 
  predict(lung, type = "survival", eval_time = c(100, 200)) %>% 
  bind_cols(lung) %>% 
  roc_auc_survival(surv, .pred)
#> Error in `roc_auc_survival()`:
#> ! All data.frames of `estimate` should include column names:
#>   (.eval_time), (.pred_survival), and (.weight_censored).

# workaround with augment
proportional_hazards() %>% 
  fit(surv ~ ph.ecog + age, data = lung) %>% 
  augment(lung, type = "survival", eval_time = c(100, 200)) %>% 
  roc_auc_survival(surv, .pred)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   .metric          .estimator .eval_time .estimate
#>   <chr>            <chr>           <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 roc_auc_survival standard          100     0.626
#> 2 roc_auc_survival standard          200     0.644

lapply(c("parsnip", "yardstick", "survival"), packageVersion)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] '1.3.3'
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] '1.3.2'
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> [1] '3.8.3'
```

<sup>Created on 2025-09-03 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

I am not sure whether this behavior is intended, but it makes the pipeline difficult to reuse consistently across different metrics. If it is intentional, would it be possible to introduce an argument that, when set to `TRUE`, automatically adds the relevant column?

Thanks!

title: Ordinal mode (between classification and regression)
description:
I think that a major missing gap in parsnip is explicit support for ordinal models, by which I mean **models where the response variable is an ordered factor**.

My proposal here is a follow up to [closed issue 35](https://github.com/tidymodels/parsnip/issues/35), specifically focusing on **ordinal models**. @topepo wrote:

> The main issue that I had as about how to organize the functions. In parsnip we try to have the main model functions describe the structural aspects of the model (e.g. linear_reg(), rand_forest(), etc). For the ordinal models based on generalized linear model (e.g. cumulative logits, adjacent categories etc), my thinking was to have:
> 
> ordinal_cumulative(link = "logit", odds = "proportional")
> ordinal_adjacent(link = "logit", odds = "proportional")
> and so on. My thinking is that people would probably want to look at the parallel assumption (assuming they have the right design for that) and tuning over the odd argument would be helpful.
> 
> How would you like to see these types of model organized?
> 

I am not a statistical expert on ordinal models. but I have used them in my research code and I have studied to learn about different kinds. Based on my understanding, the examples above are the kind of detail that parsnip is supposed to abstract away. I would think that users care mainly about three things:
* The function call to the model versus the mode of the model
* The broom tidier functions for model outputs (tidy, glance, augment)
* The prediction results

## Function call versus mode

In his initial thoughts, @topepo seemed to frame ordinal models as a parsnip model type with names like `ordinal_cumulative` or `ordinal_adjacent`. But fundamentally, in parsnip terms, **I do not think of an ordinal model as a model type; I think of it as a mode**, just like classification and regression are modes. An ordinal model is simply one where the response variable type is neither an unordered class nor a real number but rather something in between, an ordered category. This is borne out by his mention of various types of ordinal (glmnetcr, ordinalNet, ordinalForest, party models for trees, and brms models). Each of these would correspond to their various underlying model types, be it `logistic_reg` or `rand_forest`, with their corresponding engines. `ordinal` would simply be the mode.

I don't think that most users need to get bogged down with the underlying ordinal model, especially when their interest is primarily predictive analytics that focuses primarily on the prediction rather than prescriptive or interpretive machine learning (IML) that cares about the meaning of the predictors. (Personally, I actually do care very much about these interpretive issues, but I am trying to think about the general user.) Users who are concerned with interpretation can simply specify the appropriate engine (e.g., `MASS::polr` or `ordinal::clm` when the parallel assumption is upheld and `VGAM::vglm` when it is not).

That said, I think it would be responsible to help newer users who are not familiar with the assumptions to do the test for them and warn them if it is violated. For example, if the default engine is `ordinal::clm`, the parsnip call could automatically run a parallel assumption test on the fitted model using something like `brant::brant`. If the test assumption fails (with default p-value of 0.05), then the model fit call could print a warning alerting the user that the data fails the parallel assumption test on which the chosen (or default) model depends, with a suggestion for another engine that does not require that assumption. The test results should probably be silent if there is no problem and only warn when there is. (Of course, all of these options should be customizable with arguments that could skip the test, change the p-value threshold, or print the results regardless of the result.)

## Model outputs

Perhaps the reason that @topepo suggested distinct model types for different kinds of ordinal models is that the model outputs can be quite different. In particular, proportional (cumulative) odds models have a single coefficient for each predictor whereas other ordinal models like partial proportional or adjacent models might have as many as one coefficient per level of each predictor. But as I see it, these are details that are already handled in the Tidyverse by the `broom` package with its `tidy` function. [Specifically for ordinal models](https://haoen-cui.github.io/SOA-Exam-PA-R-Package-Documentation/broom/reference/ordinal_tidiers.html),

> tidy.clm, tidy.clmm, tidy.polr and tidy.svyolr return one row for each coefficient at each level of the response variable, with six columns

So, I don't think parsnip needs to worry about this, other than perhaps prioritizing the implementation of these engines that already have tidy handlers.

## Prediction results

Unless I misunderstand something, the operation of the `predict` function for the ordinal mode should be very similar to that of multiclass classification: there should be options to return just the predicted ordinal class or to return probabilities for each class. Please let me know if there is a fundamental difference here that I am overlooking.


So, these are my thoughts. How feasible would it be add the ordinal mode to parsnip?

title: FT Request: Reverse lookup mapping engines to supported models (e.g., show_models())
description:
Hallo!!

### The Use Case
Currently, `show_engines()` is showing which engines support a specific model (like linear_reg). However, there isn't a built-in way to do the reverse: querying an engine (e.g., "glmnet") to see all the different model types it supports across the ecosystem.

I think having a reverse lookup is super useful!
Not only does it make perfect sense when we specifically **know** which engine we need to use, but it also expands users' creativity by easily exposing them (us) to options they might not have realized were available...

### Proposed Solutions
- Dataset: Could we introduce something like a show_models("glmnet") function? Since the total ecosystem mapping is relatively small (only about 146 rows on the [website](https://www.tidymodels.org/find/parsnip/) currently), perhaps this underlying dataset could be exposed or queried natively within the package?

- Enhanced Error Handling / Documentation: Another thought is that it would be amazing to just include [Search parsnip models](https://www.tidymodels.org/find/parsnip/) table into error handling (with the extra .onlcick feature that i think only available for core R dev packages). 

- Enhence `show_engines()` docs: right now the docs are pretty minimal (lucky for me i was interested in glmnet/linear_reg for l1/l2 stuff) but it could be useful to at least include the possible models out there. 

Merci, Toda, and thank you veryyy much!
Yann

title: simplified tuning parameter definitions, tunable methods, engine arguments, and external packages.
description:
Related to #826 and #1104. 

I think I have a solution for the tuning parameters issues that uses the current version of parsnip. 

- For modifying aspects of existing parameters, we can add arguments such as `range` or `values` when `set_model_arg()` is called. 
- For engine parameters, register them like any other parameters. 

Both of these activities can be done in parsnip or in an extension package, and our existing machinery works as-is. 

This would solve #826 and the messiness shown in #1104 (but may not help with the issue mentioned in #1104). Overall, our code will be more simple. 

To demonstrate, I created a fake package, GlamNet, that registers a model of the same name (there is no model function) that mimics glmnet. 

It has an engine argument called `glitter_amount`  and that dials function is in GlamNet. 

GlamNet registers the arguments `penalty`, `mixture`, and `glitter_amount`. `mixture` is defined to have a truncated range of c(0.9, 1.0). 

Here's an example that shows that registration works, the new mixture range is intact, and that the machinery knows that the glitter parameter is not a main argument: 

``` r
library(tidymodels)

before <- get_from_env("linear_reg_args") |> print(n = Inf)
```

title: Registering `tunable()` information from an extension package?
description:
To make engine arguments tunable, we currently modify the `tunable()` method for the corresponding model type to include a call to `parsnip:::add_engine_parameters()` with the info on how to match the arguments with dials objects.

More and more engines live in parsnip extension packages and making their args tunable thus requires changes to parsnip. It would be helpful if that info could be provided via the extension package without needing to modify parsnip.

parsnip already carries a "database" in form of various tibbles with fundamental information about the models which gets modified by extension packages by calls to `set_engine()` etc. Can the same idea be applied to the tunable information?

title: Error when using the predict function
description:
Hello to all, 

## The problem

I  have been using the excellent parsnip package, I have been running some simulations to assess the effects of changing the regularization parameter. Now, there are cases in which I get the following message: 

Error in `.check_glmnet_penalty_predict()`:
! The glmnet model was fit with a single penalty value of 10. Predicting with a value of 10 will give incorrect results from `glmnet()`.
Run `rlang::last_trace()` to see where the error occurred.

This even though In all the simulations I am using the same penalty value of 10.  Here post I reproducible example, all the simulations run smoothly but for some reason,  the 120th simulation (that uses the same data generating process and parametrization) gives me this error. 


## Reproducible example

```r
## copy your code to the clipboard and run:
reprex::reprex(si = TRUE)

library(tidymodels)
asses_cv<-1
n_folds<-1
pen_val<-seq(from=10,to=10,length.out=1)
tuning_g<-expand_grid(penalty=pen_val,mixture=c(1))
for (i in 1:120){
  set.seed(i)
  x1<-rnorm(100)
  x2<-rnorm(100)
  y<-3+rnorm(100)
  
  train<-tibble(y,x1,x2)
  lm_elne<-linear_reg(penalty = tune(),mixture = tune()) %>%
    set_engine("glmnet",path_values = pen_val,thresh=1E-25)
  
  rec<-recipe(y~.,train)
  
  folds<-rolling_origin(train,initial = (NROW(train)-n_folds-asses_cv+1),assess = asses_cv)
  
  wf_elne<-workflow() %>%
    add_model(lm_elne) %>%
    add_recipe(rec)
  
  lm_elne_res<-tune_grid(wf_elne,resamples=folds,grid=tuning_g,metrics = yardstick::metric_set(rmse))
  
  wf_elne %>%
    finalize_workflow(select_best(lm_elne_res,metric = "rmse")) %>%
    fit(train) %>%
    predict(train[1,])
  print(i)
}


```

I would appreciate any comment. 

Thank you very much,

title: Bug (?) in `predict_class`
description:
## The problem

I registered my own parsnip model for classification.
In `set_pred`, I used a `post` function to post-process my results into the expected form like this:

```r
 post = function(x, object) {
        prob_to_class_2(x[,1], object)
      },
```

where `prob_to_class_2` is a reimplementation of parsnip's (not exported) function:

```r
prob_to_class_2 <- function(x, object) {
    x <- ifelse(x >= 0.5, object$lvl[2], object$lvl[1])
  parsnip::format_class(unname(x))
}
```
However, this gave me the following error:

```
Warning: Unknown or uninitialised column: `values`.Error in `$<-` at parsnip/R/predict_class.R:51:9:
! Assigned data `factor(as.character(res$values), levels = object$lvl, ordered = object$ordered)` must be compatible with existing data.
✖ Existing data has 8 rows.
✖ Assigned data has 0 rows.
ℹ Only vectors of size 1 are recycled.
Caused by error in `vectbl_recycle_rhs_rows()` at tibble/R/subassign-backend.R:35:5:
! Can't recycle input of size 0 to size 8.
Run `rlang::last_trace()` to see where the error occurred.
```

After looking at parsnip's source code, I think I know what is going on:

https://github.com/tidymodels/parsnip/blob/04d1bc97aa029860a20caee6bc556e1135428ba4/R/predict_class.R#L37-L56

Although the object returned by parsnip::format_class is a data.frame with 1 column, the first column isn't a factor but characters. Therefore, the first condition fails, and control is given to the else branch, trying to access a non-existent column `res$values`.

title: Add an lmrob engine for robust regression to linear_reg()
description:
[`lmrob` function documentation](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/robustbase/refman/robustbase.html#lmrob)

Notes on making a new engine at [tidymodels.org](https://www.tidymodels.org/learn/develop/models/)

## Checklist for adding a new engine

* [ ] Write the initial functions that will populate the parsnip model “database”. For example,	`parsnip::set_fit()` and so on. Suggested file name: `{model_name}-data.R`. [[example]](https://github.com/tidymodels/censored/blob/efbb1cf3b2ba8bca5de65acc3c8b665dec35631c/R/decision_tree-data.R#L13-L83)
* [ ] Engine-specific tuning parameters: Necessary parameter objects [[example]](https://github.com/tidymodels/dials/blob/d47dc47f42ad9c190d7f4a1ec85db0e385345ec0/R/param_num_knots.R) should go into *dials* and the `tunable()` method [[example]](https://github.com/tidymodels/parsnip/blob/bdc28548fd46493b52b408b6c1e04e1f80d0abdf/R/tunable.R#L338-L345) should go into parsnip. This needs a tibble which links engine arguments to dials parameter objects [[example]](https://github.com/tidymodels/parsnip/blob/bdc28548fd46493b52b408b6c1e04e1f80d0abdf/R/tunable.R#L206-L215).
* [ ] Optionally create methods for `translate()` and `check_args()` to handle engine-specific cases. These `.{model name}` methods should go into parsnip, even if the engine is defined in an extension package, as they may contain code for various engines distributed across multiple extension packages. [(example)](https://github.com/tidymodels/parsnip/blob/c54f07b7e1f7ce164aab8f95bc7b1356b68558c8/R/proportional_hazards.R#L85:L98')
* [ ] Write unit tests for the engine-specific features. 
* [ ] Write unit tests for model-specific features which require an engine. If parsnip does not contain _any_ engines for the model, put these in the extension package.
* [ ] Write the engine-specific documentation. This documentation always goes into parsnip, regardless of where the engine is defined. See the [README](https://github.com/tidymodels/parsnip/blob/main/inst/README-DOCS.md) for the parsnip documentation system.
* [ ] If the engine is added in parsnip, update `vignettes/articles/Examples.Rmd`. If the engine is added in an extension package: does it have a corresponding article that needs updating? Does the README list available models/engines and needs updating?
* [ ] Add a documentation entry in `NEWS.md`.

title: S3 Method `predict._elnet` seems to take priority over `predict.model_fit` and registered predict modules for glmnet based models
description:
## The problem

When registering a custom model which also returns a modified glmnet class object, it took me a while to notice that parsnip also exports the S3 Method `predict._elnet`. Since `_elnet` is the first listed class object in the list of class attributes, the method `predict._elnet` exported by parsnip seems to take priority over parsnip's own `predict.model_fit`, therefore never actually calling my registered predict module, but parsnips `glmnet` routine. I know that this must be some super rare edge case, but it just took me an hour to figure this out and it seems like a developer pitfall to be aware of.

```
class(my_model)
[1] "_elnet"    "model_fit"
```

title: one-class SVM with `kernlab` fails to produce predictions
description:
## The problem

I'm having trouble with using `parsnip` for one-class SVMs with `kernlab` engine using  `type="one-svc"` option.
First, it seems like I cannot get the fitted model to produce any predictions (see the reprex below). Would appreciate any help with that. 

Second, unlike `kernlab`, it seems that the only way to fit the model with parsnip is to create a fake response column to act as the `y` in the formula, even though one-class novelty detection does not require a response variable. Is there any other way?

Thanks.

## Reproducible example

``` r
library(tidymodels)
set.seed(200)
x1 <- rnorm(200)
x2 <- rnorm(200)+2 

df<-tibble(x1=x1, x2=x2)
df_test <- tibble(x1=x1+1, x2=x2+1)

df <- df %>% mutate(DUMMY_RESPONSE_DUMMY=as.factor(rep(9999,nrow(df))))

svm_rbf_spec <- svm_rbf() %>%
  set_mode("classification") %>%
  set_engine("kernlab", type="one-svc") 
  
svm_rbf_fit <- svm_rbf_spec %>%
  fit(DUMMY_RESPONSE_DUMMY~., data=df)

predict(svm_rbf_fit, new_data = df_test)
#> Error in res$values: $ operator is invalid for atomic vectors
```

title: Parsnip's "Model already registered" error prevents attaching packages with custom models to fit_resamples and tune_grid
description:
Hello, it's me again! 🥳 

So, here is the scenario: I have a package that registers custom parsnip models `.onLoad`, and also exports a custom yardstick metric for evaluation as S3method.

Now, I want to call:

```r
library(tidymodels)
library(my_pkg)

plan(multisession)

...

cv_res <- fit_resamples(my_model, y ~ x, cv_splits, metrics = my_metric)
```

However, this fails, because my custom metric `my_metric` isn't available in the workers' environments.

Ok, so what about explicitly attaching my package then?

```r
library(tidymodels)
library(my_pkg)

plan(multisession)

...

cv_res <- fit_resamples(my_model, y ~ x, cv_splits, metrics = my_metric, control = control_resamples(pkgs = "my_pkg"))
```

This fails too - this time, because on load, my_pkgs tries to register the custom parsnip model again. However, the workers apparently receive the hidden parsnip registry object, causing parsnip to throw a "Model already exists" error.

Is there is a good solution to this problem at the moment?
`parsnip:::check_model_doesnt_exist` is not exported, so the obvious route of checking in `.onLoad` is not available.
I think, for now, I will just wrap the set_new_model calls with try?

title: Penalty + Ridge
description:
I am seeing unexpected behavior when trying to compare Ridge, Lasso, and Elastic Net (this is for a class lab and I want to make sure I'm pointing my students in the right direction). Below we create a grid of potential penalties and examine ridge (`mixture = 0`) lasso (`mixture = 1`) and elastic net (`mixture = 0.5`) -- we noticed that the penalty doesn't seem to be passing for ridge. I believe this is related to #431 and #486, and when we specify the path_values it *does* work but I'm just trying to understand whether this is expected behavior, if I am teaching students to use tidymodels + ridge do they *always* need to pass path_values for their penalties? it seems the penalty is ignored without notice (but maybe I missed something!) 

``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse))
library(tidymodels)
library(ISLR)

set.seed(7)
cv <- vfold_cv(Carseats, v = 5)

rec <- recipe(Sales ~ ., data = Carseats) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_predictors())

elas_spec <- linear_reg(
  penalty = tune(),
  mixture = tune()
) |>
  set_engine("glmnet")

grid <- expand_grid(
  penalty = seq(0.01, 0.1, by = 0.01),
  mixture = c(0, 0.5, 1)
)

elas_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(rec) |>
  add_model(elas_spec)

elas_tune <- tune_grid(elas_wf, grid = grid, resamples = cv)

collect_metrics(elas_tune) |> 
  filter(.metric == "rmse") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = penalty, y = mean, group = mixture, color = mixture)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/pCsNw99.png)<!-- -->

``` r

## with path values

elas_spec_pv <- linear_reg(
  penalty = tune(),
  mixture = tune()
) |>
  set_engine(
    "glmnet",
    path_values = seq(0, 0.1, by = 0.01)
    )

elas_wf_pv <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(rec) |>
  add_model(elas_spec_pv)

elas_tune_pv <- tune_grid(elas_wf_pv, grid = grid, resamples = cv)

collect_metrics(elas_tune_pv) |> 
  filter(.metric == "rmse") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = penalty, y = mean, group = mixture, color = mixture)) +
  geom_point() +
```

title: more quantile engines
description:
Related to #465 

The ones that come to mind are xgboost, lightgbm, and qrnn. The first and last are an easy update: 

``` r
library(parsnip)
library(bonsai)
library(qrnn)

lvls <- c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9)
```

``` r
# xgboost works out of the box

xgb_qnt <- xgb_train(
  x = mtcars[, -1],
  y = mtcars[[1]],
  quantile_alpha = lvls,
  objective = "reg:quantileerror"
)

xgb_predict(xgb_qnt, mtcars[1:2, -1])
#>          [,1]     [,2]     [,3]
#> [1,] 15.19863 21.00143 21.73931
#> [2,] 15.19863 21.00345 21.73931
```

``` r
# light gbm would need a wrapper since it only does one quantile level at a time

# fail:
train_lightgbm(
  x = mtcars[, -1],
  y = mtcars[[1]],
  alpha = lvls,
  objective = "quantile",
  quiet = TRUE
)
#> Error in `data$construct()`:
#> ! Parameter alpha should be of type double, got "0.1,0.5,0.9"

lgb_qnt <-
  train_lightgbm(
    x = mtcars[, -1],
    y = mtcars[[1]],
    alpha = lvls[2],
    objective = "quantile",
    quiet = TRUE
  )
```

``` r
# qrnn works out of the box

nn_qnt <- mcqrnn.fit(
  x = as.matrix(mtcars[, -1]),
  y = matrix(mtcars[[1]], ncol = 1),
  tau = lvls,
  n.hidden = 2,
  n.hidden2 = 2,
  n.trials = 1,
  iter.max = 500,
  trace = FALSE,
  method = "adam",
  alpha = 0.1,
  print.level = 0
)

mcqrnn.predict(as.matrix(mtcars[1:2, -1]), nn_qnt, tau = lvls)
#>       tau=0.1  tau=0.5  tau=0.9
#> [1,] 21.47180 21.59744 21.71403
```

title: boost_tree() with new xgboost and trees = tune() fails with "Out of range for tree layers"
description:
## The problem

When using `parsnip::boost_tree()` with `trees = tune()` and the new XGBoost package, hyperparameter tuning with `tune::tune_grid()` consistently fails with errors of the type

```
→ A | error:   ℹ In index: 1.
               Caused by error in `predict.xgb.Booster()`:
               ! [10:23:27] src/gbm/gbtree.h:124: Check failed: end <= model.BoostedRounds() (11 vs. 10) : Out of range for tree layers.
```

This appears to be an indexing issue where parsnip is requesting more trees than the model actually contains during the prediction phase of cross-validation.

## Reproducible example

```
library(parsnip)
library(tune)
library(workflows)
library(recipes)
library(rsample)
library(yardstick)

# Create simple data
set.seed(42)
data <- data.frame(
  x1 = rnorm(50),
  x2 = rnorm(50),
  y = rnorm(50)
)

# Create recipe
rec <- recipe(y ~ ., data = data)

# Problematic model specification
xgb_spec <- boost_tree(
  trees = tune(),  # This parameter causes the issue
  engine = "xgboost", 
  mode = "regression"
)

# Create workflow
wf <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(rec) %>%
  add_model(xgb_spec)

# Create CV folds
cv_folds <- vfold_cv(data, v = 2)

# Simple grid
grid <- data.frame(trees = c(5, 10))

# This produces the error:
result <- tune_grid(
  wf,
  resamples = cv_folds,
  grid = grid,
  metrics = metric_set(rmse)
)
```

```r
all_files <- fs::dir_ls("man/rmd/", regexp = "Rmd") |>

names(case_weights)[!case_weights]

names(reqs)[!reqs]
```

title: Error with gpu-enabled `xgboost`
description:
## The problem

I am getting an error message when implementing `tidymodels` functions for `xgboost` boosted tree model with GPU acceleration. Error reports problem with `evals` parameter in [`xgb.train`](https://github.com/dmlc/xgboost/blob/766bfccb8655c5fd53eca966c109f86a3cbc1daf/R-package/R/xgb.train.R#L20)

## Reproducible example

Utilizing GPU-enabled `xgboost` version [`2.1.3`](https://github.com/dmlc/xgboost/releases/tag/v2.1.3), accessed from [Releases](https://github.com/dmlc/xgboost/releases).
Package installation:
```sh
# Build and install xgboost with GPU support
wget https://github.com/dmlc/xgboost/releases/download/v2.1.3/xgboost_r_gpu_linux_2.1.3.tar.gz    
Rscript -e "install.packages(c('data.table', 'jsonlite'))"
R CMD INSTALL ./xgboost_r_gpu_linux_2.1.3.tar.gz

```
Reprex with `credit_data` example data:
```r
> library(xgboost); library(tibble); library(rsample); library(dplyr); library(purrr); library(parsnip); library(recipes); library(workflows); library(dials); library(tune); library(yardstick); library(tidymodels)
> data(credit_data, package = "modeldata")
> credit <- credit_data |> tibble::as_tibble()
> credit_split <- rsample::initial_split(
          credit, prop = 0.8, strata = "Status"
        )
> train <- rsample::training(credit_split)
        test <- rsample::testing(credit_split)
> cv_split <- rsample::vfold_cv(
          train, v = 5, repeats = 2, strata = "Status"
        )
> scaler <- train |>
          dplyr::count(Status) |>
          dplyr::pull(n) |>
          purrr::reduce(`/`)
> xg_spec <- parsnip::boost_tree(
          mode = "classification",
          trees = parsnip::tune(),
          tree_depth = parsnip::tune(),
          sample_size = parsnip::tune()
        ) |>
          parsnip::set_engine(
            "xgboost",
            params = list(tree_method = "gpu_hist"),
            scale_pos_weight = scaler
          )
> rec_xg_flow <- recipes::recipe(Status ~ ., data = train) |>
          recipes::step_unknown(
            all_nominal_predictors(), new_level = "missing"
          ) |>
          recipes::step_novel(all_nominal_predictors(), new_level = "Unseen") |>
          recipes::step_other(all_nominal_predictors(), other = "Misc") |>
          recipes::step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors(), one_hot = TRUE)
> xg_flow <- workflows::workflow(
          preprocessor = rec_xg_flow, spec = xg_spec
        )
> xg_trees <- dials::trees(range = c(10, 300))
        xg_tree_depth <- dials::tree_depth(range = c(2, 8))
```
